title: The Broken Covenant and the Plot at Anathoth
summary: God tells Jeremiah to proclaim the words of the covenant made at the exodus and to announce that Judah has broken it by following other gods, so its curses will now fall. Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for the people. Then the LORD reveals that the men of Jeremiah's own hometown, Anathoth, are plotting to kill him, and Jeremiah, who had been like a lamb led to slaughter, commits his cause to God.
story: Chapter 10 ended with a prayer for correction. Chapter 11 explains why correction has become unavoidable: Israel was bound to the LORD by covenant, and Judah has walked away from it. The chapter reaches back past the kings to Sinai and the exodus, the founding promise “you will be My people, and I will be your God”, and says that the present crisis is that promise's curses coming due. Then the story turns personal. For the first time the book lets us hear Jeremiah speak to God about his own suffering, in the first of the passages scholars call his confessions (11:18-12:6). The man who carries God's word against his people now finds his own people, even his kinsmen, ready to cut him off.
historical:
Many interpreters connect the chapter's covenant language with King Josiah's reform. In 622 BC, the eighteenth year of Josiah, a book of the law was found during repairs to the temple, and the king led the people in renewing the covenant and purged the shrines of Baal and other gods (2 Kings 22 to 23). Most scholars identify that book with Deuteronomy or a form of it. Jeremiah began preaching a few years before, and some read verses 1 to 8 as his support for the reform's call to covenant loyalty. Others place the chapter later, under Jehoiakim, when the reform's gains had collapsed and the “conspiracy” of verse 9 had brought back the old gods. The text itself doesn't give a date, and both settings are possible.

Anathoth was a town of priests in the territory of Benjamin, a few miles northeast of Jerusalem, and Jeremiah's birthplace (1:1). It had a long association with the priestly family of Abiathar, whom Solomon banished there (1 Kings 2:26). Why its men wanted Jeremiah dead is not stated. Some suggest that his support for Josiah's centralizing of worship in Jerusalem threatened the livelihood of local priests; others think his preaching of disaster simply shamed his family. The threat in verse 21 shows that they wanted him silenced, not only punished.
cultural:
A covenant in the ancient Near East was a binding agreement, often between a great king and a lesser people, sealed with an oath and backed by blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal. Israel's covenant with the LORD follows this pattern, and Deuteronomy spells out its curses at length. Verse 3, “Cursed is the man who does not obey the words of this covenant”, echoes Deuteronomy 27, where the people answer each curse with Amen, and Jeremiah's own “Amen, LORD” in verse 5 stands in that tradition. The “iron furnace” (verse 4) is Deuteronomy's image for slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 4:20), and the land “flowing with milk and honey” is the standard description of the promised land from Exodus onward.

The command not to pray for the people (verse 14, repeating 7:16) cuts against everything a prophet was for. Prophets were intercessors: Abraham, Moses, and Samuel all stood between the people and judgment. The “consecrated meat” of verse 15 refers to sacrifices at the temple, which the people trusted to protect them. The picture of Israel as a flourishing olive tree (verse 16) draws on one of the land's most valuable crops, a tree that could live for centuries and whose oil lit lamps, anointed kings, and fed households.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 17 are prose and poetry framed as covenant proceedings: the terms are recalled, the breach is established, and the sentence is pronounced, with the refrain of hearing and obeying repeated throughout (the Hebrew verb shama, to hear or obey, occurs again and again). Verses 18 to 23 begin a new kind of material, the first of Jeremiah's laments, which continues into 12:6. It shares its form with the individual laments of the Psalms: a complaint about enemies, a statement of innocence, an appeal to God as judge, and a divine answer. The plotters' words in verse 19, “Let us destroy the tree with its fruit”, pick up the tree image from verse 16, so the fate the people face and the fate they plan for the prophet mirror each other.

outline.t: Hear the words of the covenant
A conspiracy: the covenant is broken
Do not pray for this people
Jeremiah's lament: a lamb led to slaughter
The LORD's word against the men of Anathoth

doctrines.note: The LORD's relationship with Israel was a covenant with terms, not a sentimental attachment. The same covenant that gave the land also named the consequences of betrayal, and the chapter treats both as God keeping his word.

Jeremiah's lament shows prayer as honest complaint brought to the God “who examines the heart and mind”. The ban on intercession in verse 14 shows how serious the breach has become: a time can come when judgment is already set.
Jeremiah suffers not for wrongdoing but for faithfulness, betrayed by his own town. He does not take revenge himself; he commits his cause to God.

words.note: Berit, covenant, used five times in this chapter. It names a binding relationship established by oath, with obligations on both sides. The Hebrew idiom behind “made” in verse 10 is literally to cut a covenant, which recalls the animals cut in two in the ceremony of Genesis 15. Jeremiah will later announce a new covenant (31:31), and this chapter is the background: the first one was broken by Israel, not by God.

Shama, to hear, which in Hebrew regularly means to obey as well. Verses 7 and 8 play on it: God said “Obey My voice”, and they would not obey or incline their ears. For Hebrew thought, hearing that does not change what you do is not really hearing.

Kebes, a young lamb, the ordinary animal of the sacrifices. Jeremiah calls himself “a gentle lamb led to slaughter” (verse 19): innocent, trusting, and unaware of the knife. The same picture of the innocent sufferer appears in Isaiah 53:7.

christ: Two threads run from this chapter to Jesus. The first is the covenant: Israel's breaking of the Sinai covenant is the backdrop for the new covenant Jeremiah will announce in chapter 31, which Jesus claims at the Last Supper when he speaks of the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20). The second is the innocent sufferer. Jeremiah, rejected by his hometown and plotted against by his own, like “a gentle lamb led to slaughter”, anticipates the pattern that Jesus fulfilled: rejected at Nazareth (Luke 4:28-30), betrayed by one of his own, and led as a lamb to death. The link is a pattern, not a direct prediction. There is also a difference. Jeremiah asks to see God's vengeance on his enemies; Jesus, facing his, prays for their forgiveness (Luke 23:34).

hard.q: Why would God forbid Jeremiah to pray for the people?
hard.a: It is one of the hardest lines in the book, and it comes three times (7:16; 11:14; 14:11). It does not mean prayer is useless or that God has stopped caring; the very next chapters show God grieving over his people. The sense is that the verdict on this generation has been reached, and intercession will not reverse the coming disaster, much as a physician may say that treatment can no longer prevent what is coming. Some interpreters also note that the people's own prayers in verse 11 were not repentance but panic, and that God will not be used as one more god to call on in a crisis. Jeremiah in fact keeps praying for them in chapter 14, and God answers him honestly. The command is less a wall than a sign of how late the hour is.

questions: The people trusted sacrifices and the temple to protect them while they served other gods. Where might religious practice become a substitute for obedience in your life?
Jeremiah was betrayed by his own hometown. How do you respond when opposition comes from people close to you?
Jeremiah committed his cause to God rather than taking revenge. What would it look like to hand a wrong done to you over to God's justice?
